LLM self-play algorithms have the potential for unbounded learning, where a Conjecturer model generates problems for a Solver, allowing both to improve together. However, current LLM self-play methods struggle to scale effectively with larger models or more complex tasks.

The paper proposes a self-guidance mechanism that enhances the scalability of self-play by allowing the Conjecturer to provide more informative feedback to the Solver. This approach leads to improved performance in various tasks, demonstrating that self-guidance can significantly enhance the learning process in self-play scenarios.

clean_summary: Reliable verification of proofs remains a challenge for training and evaluating AI systems on complex mathematical reasoning. Fully formal proofs in languages like Lean are easy to verify due to their unambiguity and modularity. However, most proofs are informal or semi-formal, making verification difficult. This work explores pseudo-formalization techniques to bridge the gap, aiming to improve the automatic verification process by transforming informal proofs into a form closer to formal proofs without requiring full formalization.

- Task: Code Q&A consisting of coding questions and solutions from codeparrot/apps and CodeChef.

title: Tengyu Ma (@tengyuma)
summary:
“The length of CoT can be super long”: if I still remember the paper correctly, the CoT steps needed is linear in the number of gates needed to solve the problem, or linear in the input length for a NC1-complete problem.
I also vaguely remember that it takes exponential number of neurons in 2-layer MLP to approximate almost any functions.
(These comments above don’t mean to have any other implications / extensions to any other parts of the quoted tweets or the quoted quoted paper)
Quoting @tydsh
While CoT is super useful, I kindly disagree that blindly scaling it up is all we need.
The paper proposes a universal approximation theorem by explicitly constructing Transformer weights to fit to the family of tasks. Although the depth can be constant, the length of CoT can be super long, and we don't know whether such a weight configuration can be learned by gradient descent.
It is like "since we know 2-layer MLP can fit to any data, we just believe in it and apply it everywhere".
Humans' reasoning chains are super succinct and can capture the key factors, even for unseen problems. How such representations are learned (or constructed?) on the fly is fascinating.

Agree with all these; just adding two more
7. Add the quoted tweet into your AI system prompt
8. Ideally, spend more time on writing the paper to include the most important points -- well, the reviewer will still miss some--, so that given the paper and system prompt, AI can do 95% of the rebuttal, so you save the time from rebuttal for writing the next paper better.
Quoting @furongh
NeurIPS rebuttal deadline is around the corner 😬
I’m not an expert, but thought I’d drop my two cents on how to write a good rebuttal, especially for folks writing their first few. Hope this helps someone! 🧵👇
(And please chime in with your own tips; let’s crowdsource the wisdom 🧠💬)
1. Start with gratitude + remind them you’re awesome
Begin by echoing the reviewer’s positive feedback:
> “We appreciate that Reviewer X finds our method novel, our experiments concrete, and the topic timely.”
That’s right--remind them how much they liked you. 🥹✨
2. State the overall message early
Something like:
> “The concerns raised are mostly due to misunderstandings. We have addressed all concerns below.”
💡 Be clear, be calm, be confident. (But don’t be a jerk 😇)
3. Formatting matters more than you think
Yes, I’m talking Markdown! 🧹
• OpenReview supports it
• Number your responses like a civilized human
• Use (or something alike) to collaborate with co-authors like a team of rebuttal ninjas 🥷📄
4. Use the Bullet-point BLUF strategy
💥 Bullet Points + Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF) = Reviewer brain says thank you
Each point starts with a bolded TL;DR. Then follow up with:
• Clarifications ✏️
• New experiments 📊
• References 📚
• Logic & reasoning 🧠
5. Why BLUF works:
• One idea per bullet → no logic spaghetti 🍝
• Bolded summaries → busy reviewers (and ACs!) can skim and still get the point 🏃‍♂️💨
6. Think from multiple angles 🔍
A good rebuttal isn’t just “we disagree.”
Try:
• Clarifying
• Reframing
• Adding results
• Acknowledging edge cases
💡 Each bullet can be a different strategy. Keep it classy, keep it constructive.
Rebuttals won’t fix everything, but they can build trust, show thoughtfulness, and make your case stronger. 💪
If you’re an early-career researcher writing your first few: I see you. You got this. Keep going. 🔥❤️
These are just my thoughts. Would love to hear yours! Drop your best rebuttal tips below 👇 Let’s help each other survive and thrive 💫
